humanities_role_explanation: The benchmark uses digitized historical Czech archival documents (OCR-processed) as its text source, but the primary competence evaluated is general language understanding and semantic boundary precision (topic localization and text classification), rather than disciplinary historical analysis or hermeneutic historical reasoning.
benchmark_modalities_explanation: Evaluates models on historical Czech texts paired with textual topic names and descriptions.
analytical_tasks_explanation: Evaluates document-level topic presence (binary classification) and word-level span extraction/localization of topics (information extraction).

general_purpose_benchmark.note: Specifically scoped to the task of topic localization and text-level topic classification in historical Czech documents.

evaluates_generative_llm.note: Evaluates various generative models including GPT-5 (2, mini, nano), Llama 3 (70B, 3B), Gemma 3 (27B, 4B), and Gemini 3 Pro.

quantitative_metrics.note: Reports macro-averaged Precision, Recall, F1-score, and Intersection over Union (IoU) with bootstrap confidence intervals.

published_after_march_2023.note: The paper is a preprint from March 2026.

summary: This paper presents CzechTopic, a human-annotated benchmark for the task of topic localization in OCR-processed historical Czech archival documents. The benchmark evaluates models at both the text level (presence detection) and the word level (fine-grained span localization) using an evaluation framework grounded in human inter-annotator agreement.
key_findings: The strongest LLM evaluated (GPT-5-2) achieved a word-level F1 score of 61.1, remaining significantly below the human agreement baseline of 68.7, indicating that precise span localization remains a major challenge. Fine-tuned BERT-based models (such as RobeCzech) trained on distilled data from GPT-5-mini achieved competitive performance (up to 48.3 word-level F1), outperforming several smaller open-source LLMs.
facets_explanation: The reference answers were created by a group of human annotators in a two-phase process (topic definition and localization), but their academic or professional background is not explicitly stated. Rather than resolving disagreements into a single gold standard, the evaluation preserves each annotator's spans, computing pairwise agreement scores to evaluate models against the full distribution of human judgments (signal). The localization tasks require identifying spans within the provided historical documents based on the provided topic names and descriptions, requiring no external knowledge.
